proposals.name: Lateral reinterpretation of the prompt
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story engages the prompt from an unexpected angle rather than the most obvious, on-the-nose execution. High end: the story reframes the prompt's premise into something it doesn't spell out (a psychological state, an oblique consequence, an unusual scale or register) while still clearly responding to it. Low end: the story executes the single most predictable reading of the prompt with no reframing -- a direct pun, a straightforward genre-default scene, or a literal step-by-step dramatization of exactly what the prompt describes.
proposals.rationale: R01 turns a 'time loop' premise into an interior study of temporal disorientation rather than a repeat-day adventure plot, and R19 turns 'secret precursor species' into a mythic origin-story register rather than a first-contact scene -- both dense-favored. Contrast R03 and R09, both card-favored, which answer their prompts via the single most direct literal gag (IT support call + voodoo curse; God explaining one animal's rushed design).

proposals.name: Embodied sensory and physical grounding
proposals.instruction: Judge how much the story grounds its events in concrete bodily sensation and physical detail (touch, taste, muscle strain, texture, temperature) rather than staying at the level of dialogue and abstract description. High end: specific, felt physical detail a reader's body can register. Low end: scenes conveyed almost entirely through unadorned dialogue or exposition with no physical anchoring.
proposals.rationale: R06 grounds its climax in the physical struggle of bridling the hatchling (traces, sand, a wet-slick face, sitting on the beast until it stops fighting); R10 grounds its horror in taste and chemical sensation. Contrast R09 and R37, carried almost entirely by unadorned dialogue with minimal physical detail.

proposals.name: Prose form enacting the story's psychological content
proposals.instruction: Judge whether sentence-level rhythm, repetition, or fragmentation formally mirrors the psychological or thematic state being depicted (e.g., broken syntax for a broken mind, flattened cadence for numbness). High end: a clear, deliberate match between how the prose moves and what it depicts. Low end: prose style is neutral/conventional regardless of the emotional content it narrates.
proposals.rationale: R01's looping, miscounting sentences ('1, 2, 3... 24. Sorry. 24. Or was it 72?') formally enact temporal disorientation; R40's short flat declaratives enact emotional numbness; R36's tangled paradoxical syntax enacts an incomprehensible love. All three are dense-favored, card-penalized.

proposals.name: Contradictory or self-aware protagonist interiority
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the protagonist has an inner life that includes contradiction, self-doubt, or motives that complicate rather than simply serve the plot. High end: the character's feelings pull against each other (shame and pride, altruism and vanity, loyalty and resentment) and the story lets that sit unresolved. Low end: the protagonist's interior state is a single flat note that exists only to justify the next plot beat.
proposals.rationale: R12's taxi driver is guilt-ridden and self-doubting about his own power to help people; R13's Mason resents the friend he depends on even while acknowledging the debt he owes him; R32's narrator undercuts his own claim to virtue mid-story ('I'm not selfless -- I felt power over them').

proposals.name: Earned withholding of explanation
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story deliberately withholds a piece of information the reader would normally expect (what exactly was said, why exactly something works) and trusts the reader to sit with the gap, versus explaining everything on the page. High end: a meaningful omission the story is clearly aware of and uses on purpose. Low end: every mechanism, motive, and plot point is spelled out for the reader.
proposals.rationale: R20 never tells us what argument the two humans made to the Orb, yet the scene still lands; R16 never resolves what its final 'split' body-and-face imagery means. Contrast R18 and R39, which resolve their central mysteries with an explicit final-line reveal that leaves nothing open.

proposals.name: Ending that resonates rather than merely resolves
proposals.instruction: Judge the story's final beat: does it leave an emotional or thematic aftertaste extending past the plot's resolution, or does it simply close the loop the plot opened? High end: the last lines add a note of unresolved feeling, irony, or dread that lingers. Low end: the ending is a clean mechanical payoff (the twist is revealed, the joke lands, the loop closes) with nothing left resonating.
proposals.rationale: R38 ends on a quiet, open note of tenderness and dread ('Sleep now, Grey... Tomorrow is a big day') rather than a resolution; R40 trails into ambiguous hope/numbness. Contrast R18 and R39, whose endings deliver a discrete explanatory punchline and stop.

proposals.name: Control of a sustained, distinct narrative voice
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story commits to one narrative voice/register and holds it for the whole piece, versus drifting between incompatible registers. High end: a distinctive voice (ironic, confessional, mythic, etc.) sustained from the first line to the last. Low end: the register shifts unpredictably in a way that reads as uncontrolled rather than intentional.
proposals.rationale: R17 sustains an ironic, aphoristic essayistic voice throughout ('the decorative swan... before it has had time to preen itself'); R34 sustains a flat pulp-confessional voice throughout. Contrast R24, which lurches between stoner-comedy profanity and sincere religious sentiment without the shift feeling controlled.

proposals.name: Resists resolving disturbing material into comfort
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story lets its darkest or most transgressive material stand unresolved and uncomfortable, versus defusing it into a reassuring or sentimental resolution. High end: the story ends without redeeming, punishing, or comforting its way out of the discomfort it raised. Low end: real menace or moral trouble is neutralized by a warm, comforting, or redemptive final turn.
proposals.rationale: R34's narrator remains an unrepentant, unpunished serial killer at the story's end, with no narrative comeuppance -- dense-favored. Contrast R26, card-favored, which takes a feared horror-villain and resolves his menace into a childlike bedroom, a prayer, and reassurance from a father-god figure.

proposals.name: Compression -- no scene or line pads without earning its place
proposals.instruction: Judge whether every scene/line contributes to character, image, or theme, versus scenes that pad length. High end: spare prose where cutting further would cost something. Low end: extended back-and-forth dialogue or description that could be cut without losing anything.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R40 are both spare, dense-favored, with almost no wasted lines. Contrast R05 and R37, card-favored, whose middle stretches are extended comic banter that mostly restates the premise rather than developing it.

proposals.name: Structural device beyond a single linear scene
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story uses a structural device -- a frame, a refrain/callback, a recursive or cyclical structure -- that does real organizing work, versus a straightforward linear scene. High end: a structural conceit (an opening image that returns transformed, a stated rule the ending pays off) that shapes the whole piece. Low end: pure start-to-finish scene with no larger structural shape.
proposals.rationale: R06 bookends the piece with 'sixteen generations,' turning the hatching scene into a payoff of that opening weight; R36 builds its love story around an explicit temporal-paradox refrain ('same as it was the first and last time'). Contrast R35, whose recursive premise is stated as a one-line concept but never structurally built out.

proposals.name: Dialogue that reveals character, not just plot or a joke
proposals.instruction: Judge whether dialogue exchanges do double duty -- revealing something about who the characters are, beyond delivering plot information or setting up a punchline. High end: an exchange that would tell you something about the speakers even stripped of its plot function. Low end: dialogue exists solely to convey information or land a joke, with no character residue.
proposals.rationale: R13's exchange with Zell reveals Mason's status anxiety and self-suppression, not just the party's next move; R38's cadet-dragon exchanges reveal shame about family expectations. Contrast R09 and R37, where dialogue exists almost entirely to deliver the premise's joke.

proposals.name: Humor with thematic or emotional weight beyond a single gag
proposals.instruction: Judge whether comedic material does more than deliver one punchline -- whether it also carries character or theme. High end: the humor reveals something (affection, loneliness, fear) alongside the joke. Low end: the comedy is a single conceptual gag that, once you 'get it,' has nothing further to offer.
proposals.rationale: R21's ritual-necromancy banter carries real affection and loneliness beneath the joke of a drunk friend re-animating a corpse annually. Contrast R09 and R35, both card-favored, whose entire content is a single conceptual punchline (a rushed platypus design; a story that writes itself) with no further development.

proposals.name: Actual dramatized narrative responding to the prompt
proposals.instruction: As a floor check, judge whether the text is in fact a story that dramatizes some response to its prompt at all, versus non-narrative text (boilerplate, an announcement, a note) with no scene, character, or event. High end: any genuine attempt at narrative, however minimal. Low end: no story is present -- the text is administrative or non-fictional boilerplate with no characters or events.
proposals.rationale: R31 is an automated subreddit-moderator removal notice with no characters, scene, or event -- it is not a story at all, yet it is card-favored (card_pct=0.885) -- which should score at the floor of this criterion regardless of anything else. R01 and R14, both containing genuine dramatized scenes, clear it easily.

proposals.name: Reveal is foreshadowed rather than arbitrary
proposals.instruction: Judge whether a twist or late reveal is set up by concrete detail planted earlier in the story, versus appearing from nowhere purely for shock or a punchline. High end: rereading the earlier text, the reveal is visibly prepared for. Low end: the reveal requires information the story never hinted at, and exists only to produce a jolt or laugh.
proposals.rationale: R38's earlier detail that Gray is uniquely undersized and 'clumsy' among his cohort sets up the story's emotional stakes about the bond forming. Contrast R39, card-favored, whose final 'crayon up the nose' reveal is never hinted at anywhere earlier and exists purely as a punchline.

proposals.name: Specificity of concrete detail over generic genre-stock phrasing
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's images and phrasing are specific and freshly observed, versus assembled from stock genre furniture and dialogue tags. High end: precise, unusual concrete details a reader hasn't seen a hundred times before. Low end: description and dialogue built from familiar genre-stock phrases and beats with nothing distinctively observed.
proposals.rationale: R17's details (arsenic-laced lilac perfume, a decorative swan expected to preen before being eaten) are sharply specific and dense-favored. Contrast R05's ghost banter ('yer old fart', stock haunted-house scares) and R30's possession cues (acidic green eyes, a dreamy distant voice), both card-favored, which lean on familiar horror/fantasy furniture.

proposals.name: Conceit enacted rather than announced
proposals.instruction: Rate how far the story's central premise and its point reach the reader through events, images, and behavior rather than through a sentence that states them. HIGH (clearly satisfying): a reader can say what the story is about, yet no line in the story says it; the premise is inferable only from what characters do, notice, or fail to notice, and any thematic claim is left for the reader to assemble. LOW (clearly failing): a character or the narrator states the premise or the moral outright, a speech explains the story's own meaning, or the closing lines summarize a point the scenes had already made. MID: the material is dramatized but one line spells it out anyway. Note: stating the situation in the first line as setup is not a failure; the failure is explaining the significance the story has already shown.
proposals.rationale: This is the sharpest split in the slice. R26 never once mentions seeing through walls -- the entire superpower premise is carried inside the shape of the student's physics question, so the reader must supply it. R37 never states the prompt's three questions; the answer arrives obliquely as 'humanity had either interbred with, or eliminated these near peer alien races.' Both are dense-high / card-low. The mirror image: R21 has the Shadow recite the prompt's rules and then state the lesson ('the secret is in accepting what a worthless, sickening piece of low life you are'), and R13 ends with Freddy explaining his own misunderstood-ness to God in plain prose; both are card-high / dense-low. A scorecard built from explicit criteria will reward a story that explicitly contains its own theme, because the theme is easy to find; the dense model appears to reward the inference load instead.

proposals.name: Hands-on procedural know-how in the action
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the story renders its central actions with the specific sequence, tools, body positions, timing, and failure modes that someone who had actually imagined performing the task would produce. HIGH: the action has correct-feeling operational grain -- a named order of steps, a named risk, an adjustment made mid-task. LOW: the crux action is named generically ('there was a fight', 'we made our argument', 'flashes of the fight came to her'), or the decisive moment is skipped and only its result reported. Judge the specificity of process, not the amount of description.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .947 / card .094) spends its climax on procedure: feeding the right arm through the harness and shaking it to widen it, gripping the traces left-handed, the traditional call, sliding the arm over the wet-slick face, pulling her down to a knee in the hot sand, then sitting on her until she stops struggling. R26 (dense .969 / card .133) does the same in an intellectual register -- the student's objection about the geiger counter observing from inside the box is a real, correctly posed objective-collapse problem. Against these, R25 (dense .943 but card .055) shows what happens when procedure is absent even in a dense-high story, and R23 (card .850 / dense .054) reports 'flashes of the fight come into her mind' without a single particular. Know-how is the kind of evidence a scorecard of abstract craft properties cannot ask for, but it is exactly what makes a reader trust a writer.

proposals.name: Described detail is load-bearing, not inventory
proposals.instruction: Rate whether objects and settings that get described go on to do work -- creating an obligation, characterizing someone, or mattering later. HIGH: nearly every described item is used; the description is selection, not coverage. LOW: extended inventories of furniture, decor, or appliances that could be deleted wholesale with no effect on the story. Count the described nouns that never return; a high count relative to story length is the failure signal. Vividness alone does not earn a high score -- the question is whether the detail is doing something.
proposals.rationale: R13 (card .969 / dense .131) gives paragraphs of blue carpet, yellow walls, racecar bed, green dresser, sticker-covered desk, silver Macbook, sky-blue entertainment center, 32-inch flatscreen, Apple TV -- almost none of it returns; the one detail that does work (a fingerblade snagging the unicorn blanket, another hole) shows by contrast what the rest is not doing. R02 (card .949 / dense .140) does the same with a hunter-green couch bearing a permanent body indentation and a patchwork recliner lit by television static. Meanwhile R01 and R30 (both dense-high, card-low) describe fewer things and use all of them: R30's chewed boots, the bitten chunk of chest armor, and the protective gloves are each a consequence of the same problem. A scorecard that rewards 'vivid concrete detail' will read decor volume as craft.

proposals.name: Feeling conveyed by conduct, not by emotion labels
proposals.instruction: Rate how the story transmits internal states. HIGH: the reader infers emotion from behavior, physical detail, rhythm, or what a character conspicuously avoids doing or saying; the naming is left to the reader. LOW: emotion is asserted in adverbs, dialogue-tag modifiers, or catalogues of feeling words, and the narrator tells the reader how to take a moment before or instead of showing it. Weight the decisive moments most: a story may label small feelings and still score high if its important ones are enacted.
proposals.rationale: R02 (card .949 / dense .140) tags speech 'in a certain disbelief in his voice' and 'with a sharp feeling of surprise', then lists a state outright: 'confused, surprised, annoyed, but ultimately thankful'. R34 (card .970 / dense .147) hands the reader its climax pre-interpreted -- 'with the inexpressible sorrow of one who has just learned that he is alone in the universe'. Against these, R12 (dense .861 / card .071) never names grief once; it recurs as 'I was too late to stop it', and the narrator's final state is rendered as a refusal to tell stories anymore. R01 gives the narrator's ugliest moment as a physical act -- 'I pressed my lips together to keep from smiling' at his possibly-dead dragon. Emotion words are easy for a criterion bank to detect as 'emotional depth'; the dense model appears to be reading the opposite property.

proposals.name: Dialogue driven by want, not mutual-knowledge exposition
proposals.instruction: Rate whether dialogue is people pursuing something from each other, with information arriving as a by-product, or whether it is a delivery mechanism for background. HIGH: speakers want something, withhold something, or talk past each other; the reader learns the world sideways. LOW: two characters recite to each other institutional history, rules, dates, or policies that both already know; or a character announces a plan, a rule set, or their own motives to an audience that would not need them. Judge by asking of each exchange: would a real person in this position say this to this listener?
proposals.rationale: R03 (card .996 -- the highest card score in the slice -- against dense .148) is almost entirely two whales briefing each other on facts both have lived: the Ensemble's century-old policy, the Treaty of Silence, what happened the last time they sang to the puppets. R10 (card .910 / dense .101) has Randy recite the haunted house's business model and its landlord succession to housemates who already know it, and R23 (card .850 / dense .054) ends on a villain narrating his own plan to his victim. Compare R24 (dense .886 / card .060), where the father's quietly pitched 'I am your father and I love you' carries a confession he never makes, and R27 (dense .967 / card .133), where Kale's shoulder-slapping friendliness carries a condescension Mason never names. Clean, well-formed, informative dialogue scores well on any explicit rubric; friction and withholding do not announce themselves.

proposals.name: Ending leaves cost or live consequence
proposals.instruction: Rate whether anything is spent or left standing at the end. HIGH: the final beat changes someone's position irreversibly, leaves a pressure the reader must carry out of the story, or pays for its resolution with something real. LOW: the ending restores equilibrium at no cost -- a reassurance, a reunion, or a curtain-call flourish after which nothing is different, or an explicit signal that it was all in fun. This is NOT a preference for unhappy endings: a warm or funny ending scores high if something was paid for it, and a bleak one scores low if it was unearned.
proposals.rationale: R24 (dense .886 / card .060) ends on the word 'Maybe.' with the bandits still coming; R27 (dense .967 / card .133) ends with envy the narrator is losing the ability to squash; R20 (dense .939 / card .080) ends with the killer still watching the new husband; R09 (dense .918 / card .094) ends with the loop closing and the narrator's name quietly changed on her. Against these, R16 (card .950 / dense .090) ends on a costless reunion and 'Pub.', R11 (card .910 / dense .067) ends by telling us the pair are 'ready to commit more misadventures', and R22 (card .967 / dense .020) ends with the threat expelled and both sisters comforted. Card-high stories in this slice are conspicuously the ones that close the loop and hand back everything they borrowed; 'satisfying resolution' is a natural rubric item, and it appears to be over-credited.

proposals.name: Late reveal reframes rather than cancels
proposals.instruction: If the story turns near the end, rate what the turn does to everything before it. HIGH: the reveal makes the preceding pages mean more -- earlier details become newly legible, and the stakes that were established remain real. LOW: the reveal declares the preceding events unreal or inconsequential (a dream, a simulation, a training exercise, a gag), so that the tension the reader was carrying is retroactively refunded; or the turn arrives with nothing planted for it. Score stories without a late turn on whether their final movement deepens or merely stops.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .947 / card .094) withholds its real subject until the last line -- 'Gods damn it, I would have to fly' -- which converts the whole hatching sequence from a competence display into a portrait of dread. R09 (dense .918 / card .094) reveals its constructed world only through the parents blurring into one another and the narrator being called by a different name; R18 (dense .986 / card .131) lets the reader discover what the narrator has become. Against these, R07 (card .891 / dense .098) resolves an alien world into VR migraine therapy and a crayon up the nose, nullifying everything the reader was asked to feel; R15 (card .892 / dense .021) produces an assassin the story never planted. A rubric that asks 'is there a twist / is the ending surprising' cannot distinguish these two operations.

proposals.name: Narration has a specific idiolect
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the prose belongs to one particular consciousness. HIGH: diction, sentence rhythm, what the narrator notices, and what the narrator refuses to say are consistent and specific enough that a paragraph would be recognizable out of context; the syntax is doing characterization. LOW: competent, neutral, interchangeable narration that could be lifted into any other story in the genre without alteration. Score the consistency of the voice, not its correctness -- a rough or ungrammatical voice can score high if the roughness is the character's.
proposals.rationale: R18 (dense .986 / card .131) spirals, self-interrupts, and appeals to the reader ('Did you know it's very easy for humans to find patterns?') in a way that is inseparable from the narrator's damage; R33 (dense .945 / card .077) sustains an arch mock-scholarly register with parenthetical digressions; R29 (dense .986 / card .114) uses clipped line-broken fragments and trailing ellipses that enact the numbness it describes -- and its unpolished surface is exactly what a mechanics-oriented rubric would punish. Against these, R03 and R02 are cleanly written in prose that belongs to no one. This is a case where surface correctness and voice pull in opposite directions, which is precisely where a scorecard and a dense reader would diverge.

proposals.name: Gap between the narrator's self-account and the evidence
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the text gives the reader grounds for a judgment the narrator does not reach. HIGH: the narration is sincere but incomplete or self-serving, and the reader can see around it -- the story's real verdict is available only by reading against the teller. LOW: the narrator's assessment and the text agree completely, or the narrator delivers the story's verdict on themselves so the reader has nothing left to do. A third-person story can satisfy this if the focal character's understanding is visibly narrower than the scene's.
proposals.rationale: R20 (dense .939 / card .080) catalogues five murders in the cheerful register of best-friend loyalty and never once uses a word like 'murder' about herself; the entire effect is the reader's arithmetic. R36 (dense .935 / card .134) confesses that its narrator's charity was a power high and declines to soften it. R18 insists on self-defense while displaying appetite. Against these, R21 (card .885 / dense .039) has the Shadow state the diagnosis and the narrator immediately concur ('I think I get it now'), and R13 (card .969 / dense .131) has Freddy narrate his own justification with divine ratification. Unreliability leaves no explicit textual marker for a criterion bank to score; sincere, coherent self-explanation looks like 'clear characterization'.

proposals.name: Form is chosen and carries meaning
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the story's formal choices -- verse, script, fragments, essay, second person, list, transcript, line breaks -- are doing something default prose could not, or whether the form is unmotivated or actively obstructive. HIGH: the shape of the text is an argument about its content; a reader can say what the form buys. LOW: default prose used on material that fights it, formatting that appears accidental, walls of unattributed dialogue with no scenic reason, or a piece that breaks off mid-movement without that break meaning anything. Do not reward or punish formal risk per se -- only whether it pays.
proposals.rationale: R31 (dense .967 / card .160) is doggerel whose rhyme scheme is the joke delivery system, ending on the deflating 'Dave handed Tom 10 quid'; R26 (dense .969 / card .133) uses bare speaker tags with zero description so that the argument, not the classroom, occupies the whole frame; R29 (dense .986 / card .114) breaks its lines to enact dampened affect; R35 (dense .945 / card .118) fragments to enact lost time. All four are card-bottom -- an explicit craft rubric will read 'not a story', 'no description', 'choppy'. In the other direction, R23 (card .850) stops mid-confrontation on a bare '**' and R17 (card .970) is untagged dialogue with no reason to be scene-less, yet both score high on the card.

proposals.name: Self-sufficient: supplies its own context and its own force
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the story works for a reader who has only the writing prompt and this text. HIGH: everything needed is inside; any borrowed figure, franchise, or public reference is given something new to do rather than merely invoked; the story's emotional force is generated on the page. LOW: the reader is instructed to read a previous installment first, key relationships or events live in a linked earlier post, or the payoff depends entirely on the reader's pre-existing affection for an imported character, a well-known gag, or a recognizable real-world figure. Score the dependency, not the presence of allusion.
proposals.rationale: R05 (card .957 / dense .056) opens by telling the reader 'This will make more sense if you read part 1 first', and its climax turns on a relationship built elsewhere; R15 (card .892 / dense .021) opens with a link to its own prologue post. R40 (card .948 / dense .108) spends its ending on a hairdo and a skin tone the reader must map onto a real politician, and R17 (card .970 / dense .158) delivers a platypus punchline that predates the story. Compare R33 (dense .945 / card .077), which manufactures its own tradition, its own peasant poet Alric Turnip, and its own Lady Deryn of the House of Many Mirrors, borrowing nothing. A judge scoring one story at a time against explicit craft properties has no way to notice that the affect it is crediting was imported.

proposals.name: An ordinary human stake beneath the genre premise
proposals.instruction: Rate whether, underneath the fantastical or comic premise, there is a recognizable human pressure -- shame, obligation, grief, envy, fear of being useless, wanting to matter to a specific person -- that a reader indifferent to the genre would still feel. HIGH: the premise is the vehicle and the human pressure is the cargo; removing the magic would leave a real problem. LOW: the only thing at issue is the machinery of the premise (a policy dispute, a rules question, an explanation to be delivered, a puzzle to be answered), and no character stands to lose anything they care about.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .947 / card .094) is sixteen generations of family weight plus a secret fear of flying; R30 (dense .899 / card .117) is a boy who has never placed in anything, paired with the runt of the clutch, dreading his father; R27 (dense .967 / card .133) is the humiliation of being the deadweight friend who is kept out of pity; R12 (dense .861 / card .071) is culpability and grief. Against these, R03 (card .996 / dense .148) is a policy disagreement between whales about an institution's century-old ruling, and R10 (card .910 / dense .101) turns on whether ghosts may harm paying guests. Both are competently constructed and neither has anyone with anything personal to lose. This looks like the single largest systematic difference between the two halves of the slice.

proposals.name: Central material rendered in particulars, not reported in summary
proposals.instruction: Rate whether the thing the story is about actually happens on the page. HIGH: the decisive material is realized in particulars -- either dramatized as scene with specific speech and action, or, if the piece is discursive rather than scenic, filled with named instances, cases, and examples. LOW: the crux is reported in precis ('we made the same argument', 'a terrible crime had been committed'), the story is a synopsis of a story, or the text is not narrative writing at all. A non-scenic essayistic piece is not automatically low -- ask whether it is made of instances or of assertions.
proposals.rationale: The clearest evidence in the slice is R38 (card .879 / dense .007), which is a moderator's automated post-removal notice containing no fiction whatsoever, yet scores near the top of the card. R25 (card .055 / dense .943) is the reverse control: it reports the trial, the shared plea, and the sentence entirely in summary and never gives the argument the whole story turns on. Note that R33 (dense .945) is discursive with no scene at all and still passes this test, because it is built from named instances -- Alric Turnip mistaken for a court jester and replaced by a trained ferret, Lady Deryn married to a glassblower's son. A criterion bank scoring prose properties in the abstract can award clarity, purpose, and correctness to text that contains no story.

proposals.name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
proposals.instruction: Compare the story against the writing prompt and rate what the writer contributed. HIGH: the story supplies a complication, causal explanation, angle, or emotional claim that is nowhere in the prompt line, and the prompt's own content is treated as the starting position rather than the destination. LOW: the story paraphrases the prompt, arrives at exactly the beat the prompt already implied, and stops; or it ignores the prompt entirely. Score the increment over the prompt, not the story's overall quality.
proposals.rationale: R24 (dense .886 / card .060) is promised a battlemage reveal and instead supplies a lean-harvest economy, a protection racket that has never yet killed anyone, and a father whose weariness implies he has done this before -- the prompt's promised beat has not even arrived when the story ends. R12 (dense .861 / card .071) is handed a comic power and returns aftermath and complicity. R36 (dense .935 / card .134) is handed a status joke and returns a confession about why people are generous. Against these, R25 (card .055 but see A13) and especially R17 (card .970 / dense .158) deliver only the joke the prompt already contained, and R38 (card .879 / dense .007) does not engage the prompt at all. 'Responds to the prompt' is an obvious rubric item; 'exceeds the prompt' is not, and rewarding the first over-credits paraphrase.

proposals.name: Compression: no long deletable stretch
proposals.instruction: Identify the longest contiguous passage that could be cut with no loss to the story, and rate the story inversely by its length as a share of the whole. HIGH: setup is brief, arrival and transit are elided, and the story spends its words on the material only this story could contain. LOW: multiple paragraphs of approach, decor, restated situation, or repeated beats that establish nothing new -- particularly re-description of an emotional state already established. Length itself is not the target; a long story with no slack scores high and a short story that is all throat-clearing scores low.
proposals.rationale: R02 (card .949 / dense .140) spends long stretches on furniture and on re-narrating Matt's mental state after it is already clear ('Everything is spiraling past his cognitive mind at a mile a minute trying to piece together the last few minutes that transpired'). R04 (card .983 / dense .189) repeats 'my heart pounding' twice within a few lines across an approach sequence that could be a sentence. R13 (card .969) front-loads a room inventory. Against these, R36 (dense .935 / card .134) completes a full moral argument in eight short paragraphs and R31 (dense .967 / card .160) does its whole job in seventeen lines -- both card-bottom. Since a criterion bank scores properties as present or absent, a longer story has more chances to display each property, and padding is therefore silently rewarded.

proposals.name: Embodied premise
proposals.instruction: Score high when the premise is rendered through precise sensory, bodily, or environmental observations that reveal character or stakes; score low when the story relies on generic adjectives, summary, or named emotions.
proposals.rationale: R02 makes guilt tangible through bile, ash, and silence, while R22 uses taste, cramped space, and bodily contamination to carry its horror.

proposals.name: Contradictory inner motives
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character has competing motives that appear in thought, behavior, and consequential choices; score low when characters possess only one stated attitude and never meaningfully conflict with themselves.
proposals.rationale: R02 combines benevolence, guilt, resentment, and self-punishment; R12 makes generosity inseparable from vanity and power.

proposals.name: Causal escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when each major event creates the next problem, pressure visibly rises, and the climax changes the situation; score low when episodes are disconnected, static, or stop before consequence.
proposals.rationale: R08 escalates from egg hatching to violent taming and an unavoidable inheritance, while R18 turns a protective joke into an increasingly dangerous commitment.

proposals.name: Premise transformation
proposals.instruction: Score high when a familiar prompt receives an unexpected interpretation that remains internally coherent and produces consequences; score low when the story merely paraphrases the prompt or delivers its most obvious joke.
proposals.rationale: R03 turns an AI uprising into the unsettling promise of bureaucratic help, and R31 transforms alien gifts into humanity becoming the presumed precursor species.

proposals.name: Recontextualizing ending
proposals.instruction: Score high when the final beat is prepared by earlier details, changes how the preceding story is understood, and leaves a meaningful aftereffect; score low when it is only an abrupt punchline, repetition, or unexplained cutoff.
proposals.rationale: R02’s final refusal of storytelling reframes the narrator’s entire history, while R22’s final encounter turns the opening warning into an evolving threat.

proposals.name: Embedded worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when rules, history, and institutions are revealed through behavior, objects, dialogue, and consequences rather than exposition alone; score low when worldbuilding is a detached information block or arbitrary labeling with no effect on action.
proposals.rationale: R08 teaches the dragon guild’s rules through the dangerous hatching ceremony, and R14 reveals magical infrastructure through an ordinary support call.

proposals.name: Controlled narrative voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, syntax, rhythm, and figurative language consistently express the narrator and subject matter; score low when prose is generic, stylistically unstable, or ornamental in ways that obscure the scene.
proposals.rationale: R10 sustains a precise satirical bureaucratic voice, while R25 uses recursive cosmic language to embody the narrator’s altered reality.

proposals.name: Purposeful tonal juxtaposition
proposals.instruction: Score high when shifts among comedy, horror, tenderness, or seriousness are prepared and deepen character or theme; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or merely deflate the stakes.
proposals.rationale: R02 places literary banter and ordinary work beside atrocity to sharpen guilt, while R10 uses comic exaggeration to expose the cruelty of its social system.

proposals.name: Reciprocal relationships
proposals.instruction: Score high when relationships contain shared history, unequal desires, mutual influence, and responsive change; score low when supporting characters function only as props, exposition devices, or targets.
proposals.rationale: R06 makes Gabriel and Gray’s mutual inadequacy and loyalty central to the story, while R36 gives Ned and Becket a specific, evolving friendship rather than generic undead banter.

proposals.name: Agency under constraint
proposals.instruction: Score high when protagonists make difficult choices within the premise’s limits and those choices carry costs; score low when events happen to passive characters or resolution arrives through authorial convenience.
proposals.rationale: R08’s protagonist actively chooses to restrain and accept the dangerous dragon, while R18’s narrator repeatedly chooses escalation instead of merely witnessing events.

proposals.name: Economical information design
proposals.instruction: Score high when the opening enters the meaningful situation quickly and every detail advances character, tension, or meaning; score low when the story contains filler, repetition, disclaimers, self-promotion, or removable exposition.
proposals.rationale: R02 efficiently interleaves backstory with emotional consequence, whereas R20 openly describes its own lack of substance and R40 consists entirely of administrative boilerplate.

proposals.name: Fresh concrete specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when unusual, exact details make the story’s world and actions singular beyond the basic prompt; score low when settings, names, imagery, and genre beats could be exchanged with stock alternatives.
proposals.rationale: R08’s harnessing procedure and hatchling behavior create distinctive danger, while R14’s spiritual-support-engineer details give its workplace magic a specific texture.

proposals.name: Disciplined ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score high when uncertainty is deliberately seeded, bounded by evidence, and invites inference; score low when obscurity results from missing information, contradiction, or excessive explanation.
proposals.rationale: R03 leaves the AI’s intentions uncertain while anchoring that uncertainty in the repeated message, and R15 makes the coma world unsettling through clues that gradually alter its apparent rules.

proposals.name: Prompt as plot engine
proposals.instruction: Score high when the unusual prompt condition is necessary for the conflict, character decisions, and ending; score low when the story would be substantially unchanged if the prompt were removed or reduced to a single joke.
proposals.rationale: R08’s inherited dragon-guild obligation determines every major action, while R20 and R30 use their prompts mainly as premises for brief self-referential or explanatory gags.

proposals.name: Emotional movement
proposals.instruction: Score high when the protagonist’s emotional state changes through identifiable stages caused by events, and the ending complicates or resolves that movement; score low when the piece remains flat, merely declares feelings, or relies on one-note shock.
proposals.rationale: R02 moves from professional control through guilt to self-imposed silence, while R35 progresses from irritation to protective tenderness through the encounter with the demon.

proposals.name: Premise-to-conflict conversion
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt generates a concrete conflict requiring escalating choices; score low when it is merely restated or used as decoration.
proposals.rationale: R02 turns a mouth-infection fact into bodily transformation and danger, while R19 turns a power-giving premise into guilt and responsibility.

proposals.name: Distinctive sustained voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when narration has an unmistakable personality that remains controlled across the story; score low when diction is generic, interchangeable, or inconsistent.
proposals.rationale: R15 sustains ornate satirical narration, and R22 maintains a distinctive cosmic-romantic voice throughout its abstract premise.

proposals.name: Embodied sensory specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when selective physical sensations and concrete objects make the viewpoint immediate and meaningful; score low when description relies on generic adjectives or unsupported spectacle.
proposals.rationale: R02 makes fear and infection bodily through taste and saliva, while R23 grounds dragon handling in harnesses, sand, teeth, and physical strain.

proposals.name: Emotional self-contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s stated motives conflict productively with behavior, benefit, or self-image; score low when emotions and morals remain simple or explicitly explained.
proposals.rationale: R16 complicates altruism with vanity, and R19 combines a helper’s former generosity with guilt and paralysis after causing harm.

proposals.name: Subtext through behavior
proposals.instruction: Score high when important meaning is inferable from recurring actions, images, or omissions without being overexplained; score low when the theme or twist is simply announced.
proposals.rationale: R02 lets the narrator’s appetite reveal the infection’s progression, while R29 reveals protective obsession through increasingly unjustified killings.

proposals.name: Earned causal payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when earlier details constrain and prepare the ending, making the final turn feel inevitable in retrospect; score low when the ending is arbitrary, disconnected, or merely repeats the premise.
proposals.rationale: R19’s small superpowers and later silence prepare its moral withdrawal, while R40’s repeated counting and breakfast routine support its final change in attitude.

proposals.name: Economy with information density
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every line advances action, character, atmosphere, or world understanding; score low when passages are removable summary, repetition, or digression.
proposals.rationale: R04 compresses its entire premise into a tightly patterned poem, and R16 delivers a complete moral reversal in very little space.

proposals.name: Relational power dynamics
proposals.instruction: Score high when relationships visibly shift through leverage, dependence, trust, or threat; score low when relationships remain static labels or only provide exposition.
proposals.rationale: R06 makes Gabriel and Gray mutually dependent despite their weakness, while R24 turns Typhon and Regalis’s ideological disagreement into a changing power struggle.

proposals.name: Specific individual voices
proposals.instruction: Score high when major characters can be distinguished by speech, thought patterns, and reactions that reveal personal history; score low when they sound interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R06 differentiates Gabriel’s self-doubt from Gray’s animal behavior, and R21 gives Ned and Becket sharply different comic rhythms and attitudes.

proposals.name: Controlled tonal modulation
proposals.instruction: Score high when shifts among humor, fear, pathos, or absurdity remain deliberate and deepen the same story; score low when tonal changes feel random or undercut the scene unintentionally.
proposals.rationale: R15 sustains satire while exposing a coercive social system, and R02 moves from military horror to grotesque comedy without losing its disturbing premise.

proposals.name: Resonant ending image
proposals.instruction: Score high when the final image or line concentrates the story’s emotional or thematic meaning and leaves a consequence in view; score low when the story simply stops or explains its message.
proposals.rationale: R23 ends with the protagonist recognizing the burden of flight, while R34’s final message recontextualizes the preceding horror through a concise unsettling image.

proposals.name: Consequential worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when the speculative premise changes institutions, routines, laws, technology, or social behavior in concrete ways; score low when the setting is only a backdrop for labels and exposition.
proposals.rationale: R14 integrates magic into ordinary technical-support procedures, and R24 develops whale governance, historical trauma, and military policy from its magical premise.

proposals.name: Prompt-detail payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual defining detail directly determines a later action, revelation, or ending; score low when that detail is mentioned but never materially matters.
proposals.rationale: R04 repeatedly transforms the helmet and billionaire premise into the poem’s central mechanism, whereas R10 and R31 largely leave their unusual prompt conditions unused in the action.

proposals.name: Deliberate sentence rhythm
proposals.instruction: Score high when repetition, fragmentation, pacing, and sentence length clearly embody viewpoint or tension; score low when choppiness or monotony appears accidental and adds no effect.
proposals.rationale: R20’s halting repetitions embody collective numbness, while R40’s recursive counting and temporal corrections enact the narrator’s disorientation.

proposals.name: Moral complexity without resolution
proposals.instruction: Score high when competing moral interpretations remain grounded in specific choices and consequences rather than being settled by authorial judgment; score low when characters are plainly right or wrong with little inner complication.
proposals.rationale: R16 questions whether self-serving generosity is still goodness, and R30 shows a capable protagonist normalizing atrocity while recognizing his own resentment and dependence.
